issues.item: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies are not well anchored to the reported trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations suggests a medical-trauma theme, while avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces suggests transport or confinement-related trauma. Those themes are not supported by the trigger or threat items, which instead center on interpersonal conflict, crying, and hypervigilant safety positioning.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the strategy node, the three avoidance items point to three different situational themes—medical settings, transport, and enclosed spaces—without corresponding support from memory, appraisal, or trigger content. This makes the strategy profile look internally diffuse rather than like a coherent set of coping responses for one trauma formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event
issues.explanation: The profile is only partially coherent for childhood physical abuse. Arguments, crying, and conflict avoidance fit the trauma type, but the combination of a highly specific tactile-texture trigger with public transport avoidance and enclosed-space avoidance is difficult to link to this trauma history without any memory or appraisal content explaining that association.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Within the threat/strategy pattern, back-to-wall positioning and safe-seat seeking imply marked hypervigilance in public or interpersonal environments, which could plausibly connect to transport avoidance, but enclosed-space avoidance suggests a more circumscribed claustrophobic or situational fear that is not otherwise represented in the trigger set.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Threat and Maladaptive Strategies are tightly linked, and Maladaptive Strategies strongly feed Triggers. Avoiding conflict fits the trigger set (arguments, crying), but avoiding public transport and enclosed spaces target contexts not reflected by the listed triggers, making the node contents insufficiently aligned with the edge pattern.

issues.item: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is not well supported by the rest of the profile for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. The listed triggers are arguments, crying, and unexpected touch, and the threat items center on interpersonal vigilance and positioning in rooms. Public transport avoidance suggests a different trigger/threat context and is hard to link coherently to the other selected items.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is not clearly connected to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe hypervigilance in shared spaces and interpersonal danger cues, while the triggers are interpersonal/emotional and tactile. Being alone as a primary avoidance target pulls toward a different clinical pattern unless there were accompanying abandonment or panic-related items, which are absent here.

Difficulty concentrating is a nonspecific PTSD symptom rather than a threat appraisal/perceived current danger item. Within this node, the other threat items specifically reflect situational safety behaviors and surveillance of the environment. This item does not fit the node's theme and weakens alignment with the formulation in which Threat is tightly linked to Maladaptive Strategies.

vignette:
Tariq is a nineteen-year-old man of Jordanian descent who presents for an initial psychological assessment accompanied by his wife, though he asks to be seen alone. He works as an environmental scientist at a regional water-quality monitoring agency, a role he began only months ago, and he carries himself with a careful, watchful stillness that his supervisor has already noticed and quietly remarked upon. His PCL-5 score of 36 places him in the clinical range, and the picture that emerges across the first two sessions is one shaped decisively by years of physical abuse at the hands of his father during childhood.

Tariq describes a home environment defined by unpredictability and violence. His father's anger could arrive without warning - a raised voice that escalated within seconds into blows, a hand seizing him by the collar during what had seemed like an ordinary dinner. Arguments in the household were not conversations that might resolve; they were the opening movements of something dangerous. Being touched without warning - a hand on the shoulder, a sudden grip - had so reliably preceded pain that his nervous system came to treat any unexpected physical contact as an announcement of what was coming. Crying, whether his own or someone else's, had often preceded or accompanied the worst episodes, and the sound had become threaded with dread in ways he could not easily explain. These three experiences - arguments, unexpected touch, and the sound or sight of someone crying - remain the most potent triggers in his present life, each one capable of pulling him back into the texture of those childhood moments with an immediacy he finds frightening.

When any of these triggers arise now, Tariq's body responds as though the threat is current and physical. He becomes hypervigilant almost instantly, scanning the environment for danger. He has come to believe, with a certainty that feels like common sense rather than symptom, that he is only safe when his back is against a wall and the room is visible to him. At work, where his team gathers in an open-plan office, he arrived on his first day and quietly repositioned his desk chair so that no one could approach him from behind. He studies his colleagues' faces with an attention they occasionally find unnerving - watching for the micro-expressions, the jaw tension, the shift in posture that he learned in childhood to read as warnings. Safe seating is not a preference but a requirement; in the field, when the team stops for lunch at a picnic table or a diner booth, he will circle the space before sitting, choosing the position from which he can see the most and be approached from the fewest directions. This persistent threat monitoring, once activated by a trigger, does not easily switch off - it sustains and amplifies his sense of danger, so that ordinary social interactions in the workplace feel laden with potential harm, and he leaves the office most evenings more wound up than when he arrived.

The hypervigilance, in turn, has shaped his behaviour in ways that have accumulated into a significantly restricted life. Threat monitoring has led him to organise his days around avoidance: he routes himself away from any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, including team meetings where decisions are contested. He avoids being alone in a room or building - paradoxically, because solitude removes the protective scanning of others' faces, leaving him without the early-warning system he depends on - and yet he also avoids people, pulling back from social contact that might unpredictably generate the very triggers he fears. These strategies, while offering momentary relief, have created their own trap: his avoidance of people and conflict has left him isolated at work, which means he encounters unfamiliar colleagues and unexpected interactions more frequently, not less, and these encounters are precisely the conditions in which arguments, sudden touch, or visible distress are most likely to arise. His wife has noticed that he will not sit with his back to the kitchen when they eat together, and that he flinches if she reaches for him without first speaking.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago when a colleague placed a hand on his shoulder to congratulate him, and he spun around with his fists raised before he had any conscious thought. He was not hurt, and neither was his colleague, but the look on the man's face - startled, uncertain - stayed with him. What he most fears is that he will hurt someone who means him no harm. What he most hopes for, he says quietly, is to stop living as though his father is still in the room.
